lesson.hook: Right now Earth is intercepting sunlight at a rate of about 174,000 terawatts. That figure is a short calculation: the solar irradiance above the atmosphere, about 1,361 watts per square meter, times the area of Earth’s disk, π(6,371 km)². Humanity’s total energy supply in 2025 was just over 600 exajoules, which averages to about 19 terawatts, so less than an hour of sunlight carries as much energy as civilization uses in a year. Yet solar power supplied only about 1.3 percent of world energy in 2024 on the accounting the Energy Institute now uses, and roughly 3 percent on the substitution method it used through its 2024 edition. Same panels, same kilowatt-hours, a factor of more than two. Seeing why takes units, an accounting framework and a way to draw the flows.
lesson.overview: This chapter sets up the quantitative language of the whole book. Section 1.1 separates energy from power and builds fluency in the units that energy statistics use, from the joule and kilowatt-hour to the exajoule and the quad, with a ladder of power levels for order-of-magnitude checks. Section 1.2 follows energy from primary sources through conversion to final and useful energy, starts the running example of one kilowatt-hour, and explains the three conventions for counting electricity from sources that burn no fuel. Section 1.3 teaches you to read and check Sankey diagrams, using the Lawrence Livermore chart of US energy flows. Later chapters supply the physics behind each loss you meet here: thermodynamic limits in Chapter 2, grid losses in Chapter 3, plant heat rates in Chapter 4 and capacity factors in Chapter 5.
objectives: Convert among joules, kilowatt-hours, Btu, quads, tonnes of oil equivalent and exajoules, and identify whether a quantity is energy or power.
Compute the primary energy behind a delivered kilowatt-hour from plant efficiency and grid losses.
Explain how the physical energy content, direct equivalent and substitution methods change the reported primary energy and shares of non-combustible sources.
Read a Sankey diagram, check conservation at its nodes, and extract conversion efficiencies and losses from it.

sections.title: Energy and power: units and scales
reading: Two quantities run through this whole book, and most mistakes in energy arguments come from swapping them. **Energy** is the capacity to do work or deliver heat; its SI unit is the joule (J), the work done by a force of one newton acting through one meter. **Power** is the rate at which energy is converted or transferred; its SI unit is the watt (W), and 1 W = 1 J/s [1]. Energy is a stock and power is a flow. A power plant’s capacity is a power, in megawatts (MW); what it sells is energy, in megawatt-hours (MWh). A 500 MW combined-cycle gas plant, one of this book’s two reference plants, running at full output for one hour delivers 500 MW × 1 h = 500 MWh. The same plant held in reserve all year still has 500 MW of capacity and sells nothing.

The **kilowatt-hour** (kWh) is the energy of one kilowatt sustained for one hour: 1 kWh = 1,000 J/s × 3,600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J = 3.6 MJ, exactly [1]. It is the unit on an electricity bill, and *one kilowatt-hour* is the running example we will follow from fuel to socket through the rest of the book. To feel its size, lift a 1,000 kg car with it: h = E/(mg) = 3.6 × 10⁶ J / (1,000 kg × 9.81 m/s²) = 367 m. Or heat water: at 4,186 J/(kg·K), 1 kWh warms 3.6 × 10⁶ J / (4,186 J/(kg·K) × 80 K) = 10.7 kg of water from 20 °C to 100 °C. A food Calorie is a kilocalorie, 4,186.8 J, so a 2,000 kcal daily diet supplies 8.37 MJ, or 2.33 kWh [2]. Spread over 86,400 s, that is 97 W: a person runs on roughly the power of an old incandescent bulb.

Energy statistics span so many orders of magnitude that each community keeps its own units. SI prefixes step by factors of 1,000: kilo (10³), mega (10⁶), giga (10⁹), tera (10¹²), peta (10¹⁵) and exa (10¹⁸) [1]. Electricity statistics use kWh, MWh, GWh and TWh, where 1 TWh = 10⁹ kWh = 3.6 PJ. Global statistics use the **exajoule** (EJ): 1 EJ = 10¹⁸ J / (3.6 × 10¹⁵ J/TWh) = 277.8 TWh. US agencies use the British thermal unit, defined as 1,055.056 J (the International Table Btu), and the **quad**, 10¹⁵ Btu = 1.055 × 10¹⁸ J = 1.055 EJ [2]. One quad is therefore 293.1 TWh. Write each conversion as a fraction equal to one, such as (1.055 EJ / 1 quad), and cancel the units on paper before you touch a calculator.

Order-of-magnitude reasoning comes before precision, so carry a ladder of power levels in your head (Figure 1.1). A phone charger draws about 20 W. A household that uses 10,000 kWh of electricity a year averages 10,000 kWh / 8,760 h = 1.14 kW. A large modern offshore wind turbine is rated at around 15 MW, a combined-cycle gas plant at several hundred megawatts. The world’s total energy supply in 2025, just over 600 EJ according to the Energy Institute’s 2026 *Statistical Review*, averages 600 × 10¹⁸ J / 3.154 × 10⁷ s = 19 TW [4]. Above all of these sits the Sun. Measured above the atmosphere, sunlight delivers about 1,361 W/m² [3]; over Earth’s cross-section, π(6.371 × 10⁶ m)² = 1.275 × 10¹⁴ m², that is 1.74 × 10¹⁷ W. From charger to sunlight spans 16 orders of magnitude.

Dividing an annual energy total by the seconds or hours in a year converts it into an average power, and this one step does a great deal of work in this book. The United States consumed 94.2 quads of primary energy in 2024, according to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) [5]. That is 99.4 EJ, an average of 3.14 TW over the 366 days of a leap year (worked below). With about 340 million residents, that comes to roughly 9 kW per person, against about 2.3 kW for the world, where 19 TW is shared among some 8.2 billion people. The same arithmetic, run the other way, defines the capacity factor of Chapter 5: a 200 MW wind farm, our second reference plant, that produced 613,200 MWh in a year averaged 613,200 MWh / 8,760 h = 70 MW, or 35 percent of its rating.

example.title: Worked example: US energy use in 2024 as a power level
steps: Start from the EIA total for 2024: E = 94.2 quads = 94.2 × 10¹⁵ Btu.
Convert to joules: E = 94.2 × 10¹⁵ Btu × 1,055.06 J/Btu = 9.94 × 10¹⁹ J = 99.4 EJ. As a cross-check in electricity units, 99.4 EJ × 277.8 TWh/EJ = 27,600 TWh.
Find the time. 2024 was a leap year: t = 366 d × 86,400 s/d = 3.162 × 10⁷ s, or 366 d × 24 h/d = 8,784 h.
Divide: P = 9.94 × 10¹⁹ J / 3.162 × 10⁷ s = 3.14 × 10¹² W = 3.14 TW. The cross-check agrees: 27,600 TWh / 8,784 h = 3.14 TW.
Per person, with about 3.40 × 10⁸ residents: 3.14 × 10¹² W / 3.40 × 10⁸ = 9,200 W ≈ 9.2 kW, about four times the world average of 2.3 kW.
example.takeaway: Turning an annual energy total into an average power in watts per person makes statistics in different units directly comparable and easy to check against Figure 1.1.

misconception.fact: A day’s output is energy, in kWh; kW describes how fast the panels produce at an instant, or their rated peak. A 6 kW array might produce 30 kWh on a sunny day, and “6 kW per day” mixes a rate with a time. The reverse error, “kilowatts per hour,” is a real unit (a ramp rate, which matters for power plants in Chapter 7) but is almost never what the speaker meant.

practice.q: A 2,000 W space heater runs for 3 hours. How much energy does it use?
practice.explanation: E = P × t = 2 kW × 3 h = 6 kWh, and 6 kWh × 3.6 MJ/kWh = 21.6 MJ. 6 kW is a power, 667 W is 2,000 W divided by 3 (a meaningless operation here), and 21.6 kJ is off by a factor of 1,000.

practice.q: Express 1 quad in TWh, and find the average power of an economy that uses exactly 1 quad of energy in a 365-day year.
practice.answer: 1 quad = 10¹⁵ Btu × 1,055.06 J/Btu = 1.055 × 10¹⁸ J. In TWh: 1.055 × 10¹⁸ J / 3.6 × 10¹⁵ J/TWh = 293 TWh. Average power: 293 TWh / 8,760 h = 0.0335 TW = 33.5 GW, or equivalently 1.055 × 10¹⁸ J / 3.154 × 10⁷ s = 3.35 × 10¹⁰ W.
practice.explanation: A good answer carries units through each step, uses 3.6 × 10¹⁵ J per TWh, and recognizes that energy per year is a power. The result, about 33 GW per quad per year, is a handy rule of thumb.

practice.q: A planning document says a new data-center campus will use 1 TWh of electricity per year. What average power must the grid supply?
practice.explanation: P = 10¹² Wh / 8,760 h = 1.14 × 10⁸ W = 114 MW. Choosing 1 TW confuses energy per year with power; 8.8 GW misplaces the 8,760 hours of the year and is about 77 times too large; 11.4 MW is off by a factor of 10.

sections.title: Primary energy and final use
reading: Energy statistics follow energy through a chain of forms, and every link loses something. **Primary energy** is energy as first extracted or captured from nature: crude oil, coal and natural gas as they leave the ground, the heat released in a reactor, the electricity from a wind turbine or a hydro dam. Refineries and power plants convert it into **secondary energy** carriers such as gasoline, electricity, district heat or hydrogen. **Final energy** is what end users buy and meter: liters at the pump, kWh at the meter, cubic meters of gas at the boiler. End-use devices turn final energy into **useful energy** (heat in a room, torque at a wheel, light), which provides an **energy service** such as a warm room or a kilometer traveled [1]. The International Energy Agency (IEA) reports national energy at the first and third of these stages, as total energy supply and total final consumption.

Follow one kilowatt-hour back from a socket. Suppose it came from a combined-cycle gas plant that converts 55 percent of the fuel’s heat into electricity (Chapter 2 explains how two cycles in series reach this), and that 5 percent of the electricity sent out is lost in transmission and distribution (Section 1.3 and Chapter 3). The plant must send out 1 kWh / 0.95 = 1.053 kWh and burn 1.053 kWh / 0.55 = 1.91 kWh of gas, or 6.89 MJ. Only 52 percent of the primary energy reaches the socket. What happens next depends on the device. An electric motor at 90 percent efficiency turns the kWh into 0.9 kWh of shaft work, while a heat pump with a coefficient of performance of 3 delivers 3 kWh of heat. Useful energy can exceed final energy because the heat pump moves heat drawn from outdoor air; the second law, in Chapter 2, sets how much.

For fuels, primary energy is the heat released by burning them, but even that needs a convention. The **higher heating value** (gross calorific value) includes the latent heat recovered if the water vapor in the exhaust condenses; the **lower heating value** (net calorific value) excludes it. For natural gas the two differ by about 10 percent. The IEA and most international statistics use net values, while the EIA uses gross values [1]. International statistics also report energy in **tonnes of oil equivalent**, defined as 10⁷ kcal = 41.868 GJ, so 1 Mtoe = 41.868 PJ = 11.63 TWh [1]. Chapter 4 returns to heating values when we compute a plant’s fuel cost from its heat rate; for now, note which basis any efficiency or heat rate you read is quoted on.

The hard problem is electricity from sources that burn nothing. There is no fuel to weigh, so a convention must decide what counts as primary energy, and three are in use. The **physical energy content method**, used by the IEA and Eurostat, takes the first energy form downstream for which more than one use is practical. For hydro, wind and solar photovoltaics that is electricity, so 1 kWh counts as 3.6 MJ. For nuclear and geothermal it is heat, estimated by assuming conversion efficiencies of 33 percent and 10 percent [1]. The **direct equivalent method**, used in IPCC assessments, counts every non-combustible source, nuclear included, at its electricity output [2]. The **substitution method** counts the fuel a typical thermal plant would have burned to make the same electricity: at an assumed 40 percent efficiency, 1 kWh of wind becomes 3.6 MJ / 0.40 = 9.0 MJ (Figure 1.2).

The choice moves headline numbers. The Energy Institute’s *Statistical Review*, one of the most quoted global datasets, used the substitution method through its 2024 edition, which reported 620 EJ of primary energy for 2023 [3]. Its 2025 edition switched to the physical energy content method, in line with the IEA and EIA, and reported 2024 wind and solar output of 9.04 EJ and 7.72 EJ [4]. Together that is 16.8 EJ, or 4,660 TWh, about 2.8 percent of a world total of roughly 590 EJ. Count the same electricity by substitution at 40 percent and it becomes 16.8 EJ / 0.40 = 41.9 EJ, about 6.8 percent of a correspondingly larger total. Nothing physical changed. The substitution method estimates how much fossil fuel these sources stand in for; the physical content method records the energy that entered the economy. Chapter 8 shows why the difference grows as transport and heat electrify.

US statistics went through the same change. Beginning with its September 2023 *Monthly Energy Review*, the EIA counts electricity from wind, solar and hydro at its heat content, 3,412 Btu per kWh, which is simply 3.6 MJ expressed in Btu. Before that it used **fossil fuel equivalence**, valuing each renewable kWh at the heat rate of fossil-fuel plants, a substitution method [5]. Nuclear electricity is still counted as reactor heat, through the fleet’s heat rate, so the US convention now resembles the physical energy content method. The EIA’s documentation also describes a third option, incident energy, which would count the sunlight striking a panel or the wind passing a rotor [5]. Because the Lawrence Livermore flow charts in Section 1.3 are built from EIA data, this choice sits inside every band of those diagrams.

example.title: Worked example: primary energy behind 1 kWh from gas, nuclear and wind
steps: Fix the delivered energy and the grid losses: E_del = 1 kWh = 3.6 MJ. With 5 percent losses the plants must send out E_out = 1 kWh / 0.95 = 1.053 kWh.
Gas, combined cycle at 55 percent: E_prim = 1.053 kWh / 0.55 = 1.91 kWh = 1.91 kWh × 3.6 MJ/kWh = 6.89 MJ. Gas is a fuel, so every method gives this answer.
Nuclear: the physical content method assumes 33 percent, so E_prim = 1.053 kWh / 0.33 = 3.19 kWh = 11.5 MJ. The direct equivalent method gives E_prim = 1.053 kWh = 3.79 MJ.
Wind: physical content and direct equivalent both give 1.053 kWh = 3.79 MJ. Substitution at 40 percent gives 1.053 kWh / 0.40 = 2.63 kWh = 9.47 MJ.
Compare: the same delivered kWh carries between 3.79 MJ and 11.5 MJ of primary energy, a factor of 3, depending on source and convention (Figure 1.2).
example.takeaway: Before you compare primary-energy shares from two datasets, find out which accounting method each one used.

misconception.myth: “Wind and solar are under 3 percent of world energy, so they hardly matter to the energy system.”
misconception.fact: The figure depends on the stage and the method. On the physical content method, wind and solar were about 2.8 percent of world primary energy in 2024; by substitution they would be about 7 percent. Their share of electricity generation, about 15 percent in 2024, is much higher than either, because electricity is the stage at which they enter the system. Always ask which stage (primary, final or electricity) and which method a percentage uses.

practice.q: Under the physical energy content method, how is 1 kWh of electricity from a nuclear plant counted as primary energy?
choices: As 3.6 MJ, the same as wind
As about 10.9 MJ, the reactor heat at an assumed 33 percent efficiency
As 9.0 MJ, the fuel a fossil plant at 40 percent would burn
As zero, because uranium is not a fossil fuel
practice.explanation: For nuclear, the first practical energy form is heat, estimated as 3.6 MJ / 0.33 = 10.9 MJ. 3.6 MJ is the direct equivalent treatment, 9.0 MJ is substitution, and no method counts nuclear as zero.

practice.q: A country generates 1,000 TWh of hydroelectricity in a year. Compute the hydro contribution to primary energy in EJ by (a) the physical energy content method and (b) the substitution method with an assumed 38 percent efficiency. By what factor do they differ?
practice.explanation: A good answer converts TWh to EJ correctly (1 TWh = 3.6 PJ), applies the efficiency by division, and notes that the ratio depends only on the assumed efficiency.

practice.q: A heat pump delivers 3 kWh of heat to a house for each 1 kWh of electricity it draws. Which statement is correct?
choices: Its useful energy exceeds its final energy because it moves heat from the outdoor air
Its primary energy use is 3 kWh
Its final energy use is 3 kWh
practice.explanation: Final energy is the 1 kWh of electricity; useful energy is the 3 kWh of heat, of which 2 kWh is moved from outdoors. Energy is conserved. The primary energy depends on how the electricity was generated, not on the heat delivered.

sections.title: Reading energy flow (Sankey) diagrams
reading: In 1898 the engineer Matthew Henry Phineas Riall Sankey published a diagram of a steam engine in which the width of each arrow was proportional to the heat flowing through it; the broad band of heat entering the boiler narrowed to a thin band of useful work, with the rest peeling off as losses [1]. Diagrams of this kind now carry his name. Earlier flow maps existed, most famously Charles Joseph Minard’s 1869 chart of Napoleon’s army in Russia, but Sankey made the form a tool of energy engineering [1]. A **Sankey diagram** follows three rules. Band width is proportional to quantity. All bands share one unit. And flows are conserved at every **node**, so what enters a box equals what leaves it plus any change in storage.

The best-known energy Sankey diagram is the chart of US energy flows that Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL) publishes from EIA data [2]. Read it from left to right. Primary sources sit in a column on the left: solar, nuclear, hydro, wind, geothermal, natural gas, coal, biomass and petroleum. Some flows run to a box for electricity generation; the rest go straight to the four end-use sectors, residential, commercial, industrial and transportation, which also receive electricity. On the right, every sector splits into two sinks: **energy services**, the estimated useful energy, and **rejected energy**, heat released to the environment. The units are quads, and the chart for 2023 totals 93.6 quads (Figure 1.3) [2].

The 2023 chart can be checked with arithmetic. Of 93.6 quads, 61.5 appear as rejected energy and 32.1 as energy services, and 61.5 + 32.1 = 93.6, so the diagram closes [2]. Electricity generation takes in about 32 quads of primary energy (we use 32.1 below). The four sectors receive 11.3 (residential), 9.3 (commercial), 26.1 (industrial) and 28.0 (transportation) quads, 74.7 quads in all, electricity included [2]. Fuel used directly in the sectors is 93.6 − 32.1 = 61.5 quads, so the electricity delivered must be 74.7 − 61.5 = 13.2 quads, about 3,870 TWh, and 32.1 − 13.2 = 18.9 quads leave the power sector as rejected energy. About 41 percent of the primary energy entering US power plants in 2023 reached customers as electricity.

Two cautions apply to the right-hand side. Rejected energy is not all waste that better engineering could recover: much of it is the heat that any heat engine must reject to its cold reservoir, a limit Chapter 2 derives from the second law. And energy services are not measured. LLNL estimates them by applying an assumed end-use efficiency to each sector, lowest for transportation, where most fuel burns in combustion engines, so the 32.1 quads of services is a model result [2]. Some losses are also smaller than intuition suggests. The EIA estimates that transmission and distribution losses average about 5 percent of the electricity moved through the US grid [4], while the US thermal fleet as a whole loses more than half of its fuel’s energy as heat.

Because LLNL builds its chart from EIA statistics, the accounting method of Section 1.2 sits inside every band. The chart for 2022, as first published, totals 100.3 quads [3]; the chart for 2023 totals 93.6. US energy use did not fall 7 percent in a year. Most of the gap reflects the EIA’s switch to the captured energy approach. A rough estimate shows the size: the United States generated on the order of 900 TWh from wind, solar and hydro, and re-counting that electricity at 3,412 Btu/kWh instead of a fossil-plant heat rate of roughly 9,500 Btu/kWh removes 9 × 10¹¹ kWh × 6,100 Btu/kWh ≈ 5.5 × 10¹⁵ Btu, or about 5.5 quads, mostly from the power sector’s rejected energy. Compare Sankey diagrams across years or countries only after checking that they share an accounting basis.

Sankey diagrams work at every scale, from one engine to the planet. Cullen and Allwood drew a global diagram for 2005 that follows energy from fuels through conversion devices, such as engines, furnaces and electric motors, to final services such as transport, heating and illumination [5]. To build one for a country, as this chapter’s challenge asks, start from an energy balance table: the IEA’s World Energy Balances or a national agency’s. Fix one year, one unit and one accounting method. Draw the nodes (primary sources, transformation, end-use sectors), size each band from the table, and check that every node closes to within the table’s statistical difference, the line in an energy balance that records what the data cannot reconcile.

example.title: Worked example: reading the power sector off the 2023 LLNL chart
steps: Read the input: electricity generation receives 32.1 quads of primary energy in 2023.
Read the end-use sector totals, which include electricity: 11.3 + 9.3 + 26.1 + 28.0 = 74.7 quads.
Apply conservation. Fuel going directly to the sectors is 93.6 − 32.1 = 61.5 quads, so electricity delivered = 74.7 − 61.5 = 13.2 quads. In TWh: 13.2 quads × 293.1 TWh/quad = 3,870 TWh.
Power-sector efficiency from primary energy to customer: 13.2 quads / 32.1 quads = 0.41. The other 18.9 quads, 59 percent, are rejected at plants and on the grid.
Whole economy: 32.1 quads of services / 93.6 quads of primary energy = 0.34, so about a third of US primary energy became energy services, under LLNL’s assumed end-use efficiencies.
example.takeaway: Every node in a Sankey diagram is a conservation equation, and writing those equations out recovers quantities the chart does not label.

misconception.myth: “Two-thirds of America’s energy is wasted, so better efficiency could cut energy use by two-thirds.”
misconception.fact: Much of the rejected energy is heat that the second law requires every heat engine to reject, and the services estimate rests on assumed efficiencies. Large savings come mainly from changing conversion technology, for example replacing combustion engines and boilers with electric motors and heat pumps, or thermal generation with wind and solar, which also changes how the chart is drawn (Section 1.2).

practice.q: A node in a Sankey diagram receives bands of 40 PJ and 25 PJ and sends out bands of 30 PJ and 20 PJ. What can you conclude?
choices: 15 PJ is unaccounted for: a missing outflow, a storage change or a statistical difference
The node is a power plant with 77 percent efficiency
Sankey diagrams do not need to conserve flows
practice.explanation: Inflow is 65 PJ and outflow 50 PJ, so 15 PJ is missing. Conservation must hold at every node; 77 percent is 50/65, which treats an incomplete diagram as an efficiency.

practice.q: A country’s Sankey diagram shows 4.0 EJ of primary energy entering power plants, 1.6 EJ of electricity leaving them, and grid losses of 3 percent. Compute the electricity reaching end users, the rejected energy from the power sector, and the sector’s primary-to-delivered efficiency.
practice.answer: Delivered = 1.6 EJ × (1 − 0.03) = 1.552 EJ. Rejected = 4.0 EJ − 1.552 EJ = 2.448 EJ (2.4 EJ at the plants plus 0.048 EJ on the grid). Efficiency = 1.552 / 4.0 = 0.388, about 39 percent.
practice.explanation: A good answer applies the losses to the electricity sent out, checks that 1.552 + 2.448 = 4.0 EJ, and reports the efficiency from primary energy to customer.

practice.q: Two Sankey diagrams of the same country for consecutive years show total primary energy falling from 10.0 EJ to 9.4 EJ, while final energy in every sector is unchanged. Which explanation should you check first?
choices: A sharp fall in industrial output
A change in the accounting method for non-combustible electricity
practice.explanation: With final energy unchanged, a fall in primary energy points to the conversion stage. A switch from substitution to physical content accounting, as the EIA made in 2023, shrinks primary energy without any physical change. Higher losses would raise primary energy, and lower industrial output would reduce final energy.

interactives.title: Checking the 2023 US energy flow chart
interactives.intro: You have the LLNL chart of US energy flows for 2023 (Figure 1.3). Work through each question before revealing the answer.

steps.q: The chart shows 93.6 quads entering on the left, and two sinks on the right: 61.5 quads of rejected energy and 32.1 quads of energy services. What is the first check to make?
steps.a: Closure: 61.5 + 32.1 = 93.6 quads, so the diagram conserves energy overall. Then check each node the same way, because a diagram can close overall and still be wrong inside.

steps.q: Electricity generation receives 32.1 quads, and the four end-use sectors receive 74.7 quads including electricity. How much electricity was delivered, and how efficient was the power sector from primary energy to customer?
steps.a: Direct fuel = 93.6 − 32.1 = 61.5 quads, so electricity delivered = 74.7 − 61.5 = 13.2 quads, about 3,870 TWh. Efficiency = 13.2 / 32.1 = 41 percent; 18.9 quads were rejected at plants and on the grid.

steps.q: The 2022 chart totaled 100.3 quads and the 2023 chart 93.6. Did US energy use fall by 7 percent in one year?
steps.a: No. Most of the gap comes from the EIA’s 2023 switch to the captured energy approach, which counts wind, solar and hydro electricity at 3,412 Btu/kWh instead of a fossil-plant heat rate of roughly 9,500 Btu/kWh. Re-counting on the order of 900 TWh this way removes about 5.5 quads.

steps.q: A colleague says the 61.5 quads of rejected energy prove the country could cut its energy use by two-thirds. How do you reply?
steps.a: Much rejected energy is heat that the second law requires heat engines to reject, and the services figure rests on assumed end-use efficiencies. Large reductions come from changing conversion technology (electric motors, heat pumps, wind and solar) rather than from tuning existing engines.

quiz.q: Which of these quantities is a power?
quiz.explanation: Megawatts measure a rate of energy flow. kWh, quads and MJ are all units of energy.

quiz.q: A 9 W LED bulb runs 5 hours a day for a 365-day year. How much electricity does it use?
quiz.explanation: E = 9 W × 5 h/day × 365 days = 16,425 Wh = 16.4 kWh. 45 W multiplies power by hours per day without completing the energy calculation; the other two are off by a factor of 10.

quiz.q: World total energy supply of 600 EJ in one year corresponds to an average power of about:
Under the physical energy content method, 1 kWh of electricity from a wind turbine counts as how much primary energy?
choices: Nothing, because wind is not a fuel
quiz.explanation: For wind, hydro and solar PV the first practical energy form is electricity, so 1 kWh counts as 3.6 MJ. 9.0 MJ is substitution at 40 percent; 10.9 MJ is the nuclear convention at 33 percent.

quiz.q: A coal plant converts 36 percent of its fuel’s heat to electricity, and the grid loses 6 percent of what it carries. How much primary energy lies behind each kWh delivered?
quiz.explanation: Sent out = 1 kWh / 0.94 = 1.064 kWh; primary = 1.064 kWh / 0.36 = 2.96 kWh = 10.6 MJ. 2.78 kWh ignores the grid losses.

quiz.q: Which body’s assessments count nuclear electricity at its electrical output, using the direct equivalent method?
quiz.explanation: IPCC reports use the direct equivalent method. The IEA (and the Energy Institute since 2025) count nuclear as reactor heat at 33 percent, the EIA uses the nuclear fleet heat rate, and the Energy Institute previously used substitution.

quiz.q: On the 2023 LLNL chart, roughly what fraction of the primary energy entering US power plants reached customers as electricity?
quiz.explanation: Electricity delivered is 13.2 quads out of 32.1 quads of input: 13.2 / 32.1 = 0.41. 66 and 34 percent are the economy-wide rejected and services shares.

quiz.q: A country’s Sankey diagram shows a refinery node with 5.0 EJ of crude oil in, 4.6 EJ of products out, and no other bands. What should you conclude?
choices: The refinery is more than 100 percent efficient
A band of about 0.4 EJ for refinery losses and own use is missing
Crude oil is not primary energy
The diagram must use the substitution method
quiz.explanation: Conservation at the node requires 5.0 = 4.6 + losses, so a 0.4 EJ outflow for losses and the refinery’s own fuel use is missing. The accounting method for electricity has nothing to do with a refinery node.

corrections.before: roughly 3 percent on the method it used until its 2024 edition
corrections.after: roughly 3 percent on the substitution method it used through its 2024 edition
corrections.why: The Energy Institute used the substitution method in the 2024 edition and switched in the 2025 edition (as Section 1.2 says correctly). 'Until its 2024 edition' suggests the change came with the 2024 edition. The arithmetic checks out: 7.72 EJ / ~590 EJ = 1.3 percent; 7.72/0.40 = 19.3 EJ out of ~635 EJ under substitution = 3.0 percent.

corrections.before: 8.8 GW multiplies by the hours instead of dividing
corrections.after: 8.8 GW misplaces the 8,760 hours of the year and is about 77 times too large
corrections.why: Multiplying 1 TWh by 8,760 h does not give 8.8 GW, so the explanation of this distractor is wrong (8.76 GW / 114 MW = 77). The key (114 MW) is correct.

corrections.before: Their share of electricity generation is several times higher than either, because electricity is the stage at which they enter the system.
corrections.after: Their share of electricity generation, about 15 percent in 2024, is much higher than either, because electricity is the stage at which they enter the system.
corrections.why: Wind plus solar supplied about 15 percent of world electricity in 2024 (Ember, Energy Institute). That is about five times the 2.8 percent physical-content share but only about twice the ~7 percent substitution share, so 'several times higher than either' overstates the gap.

corrections.before: Electricity generation takes in about 32.1 quads of primary energy.
corrections.after: Electricity generation takes in about 32 quads of primary energy (we use 32.1 below).
corrections.why: The secondary transcriptions of the 2023 LLNL chart I could find (Penn State EGEE 102) give electricity generation as 32 quads; I could not confirm 32.1. It is suspicious that this value would exactly equal the 32.1 quads of energy services. 'About 32.1' also claims more precision than the source supports. The derived values (13.2 delivered, ~41 percent) barely move if the input is 32.0.

corrections.before: while thermal power plants lose more than half of their fuel’s energy as heat.
corrections.after: while the US thermal fleet as a whole loses more than half of its fuel’s energy as heat.
corrections.why: This is not true of every thermal plant. The chapter's own reference combined-cycle plant converts 55 percent and so rejects only 45 percent. The statement holds for the fleet average (EIA reports total electrical system losses of roughly 18 quads against about 13 quads of retail sales in 2023).

corrections.before: The chart for 2022 totals 100.3 quads [3]; the chart for 2023 totals 93.6.
corrections.after: The chart for 2022, as first published, totals 100.3 quads [3]; the chart for 2023 totals 93.6.
corrections.why: LLNL's October 2023 release gave 100.3 quads for 2022. Commentary on the 2023 chart (Lloyd Alter) reports that 2022 was later shown at 94.7 quads on the new basis, so a learner who downloads the current 2022 chart may see a different total. That 94.7 figure supports the chapter's 'mostly an accounting change' estimate: 5.6 of the 6.7 quad gap (about 84 percent) is accounting, consistent with the 5.5 quad estimate. EIA's electrical system losses also fell from about 23.1 to 17.8 quads.

corrections.before: Nothing physical changed between those editions
corrections.after: Most of the drop is accounting; real supply grew about 2 percent in 2024
corrections.why: The comparison is 620 EJ (2023, substitution) against ~590 EJ (2024, physical content), which covers different years. World energy supply actually grew about 2 percent in 2024 (Energy Institute 2025 coverage), so it is wrong to say nothing physical changed between those two numbers. The reading's 'Nothing physical changed' refers to re-counting the same 2024 electricity and is fine.
Gas is a fuel, and the worked example and caption both say every method gives the same answer. Labelling only this bar 'physical content' suggests the value depends on the method.

corrections.before: Simplified: the split of each fuel between power plants and direct use is not shown.
corrections.after: Simplified: bands do not show which fuels feed power plants or which sectors use electricity.
corrections.why: The bands are drawn to scale correctly. Every width matches 2.8 px per quad, and the node sums 93.6, 74.7, 61.5 and 32.1 all close. However, the 32.1-quad electricity band leaves from beside the petroleum box (petroleum supplies only ~0.1 quad to US power), and the 13.2-quad delivered band enters the top of the Transportation box (transport uses almost no electricity). The current note covers only the first of these.

review.summary: The chapter is highly accurate. All 14 multiple-choice keys are correct. All calculations, unit conversions, explorer formulas and figure geometry (log-scale positions, bar lengths, Sankey widths) were recomputed and agree. Headline statistics checked out: EI 2026 (>600 EJ, ~86% fossil), EI 2024 (620 EJ), EIA 94.2 quads, LLNL 2023 totals and sector assignments (residential 11.3, commercial 9.3, industrial 26.1, transportation 28.0), EIA's September 2023 captured-energy switch, and ~5% T&D losses. The problems found are small precision and wording issues: the 'until its 2024 edition' phrasing, one distractor explanation, the unconfirmed 32.1-quad power-sector input, and two figure labels.
